summary: Describes the messages and procedures of NORM, a protocol for reliable transport of bulk data or streams over IP multicast. It uses selective negative acknowledgments, where receivers only speak up about what they missed. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 5740.

eli5.summary: A teacher reads to a big class and only repeats a part when someone puts a hand up to say they missed it. Nobody has to say they heard everything.

questions: how does norm congestion control work
subtitle: Scalable multicast file delivery using selective requests for missing packets

tldr.problem: Delivering bulk data (files or streams) reliably to many receivers over multicast is difficult because receivers cannot all acknowledge receipt individually, or the sender would be overwhelmed by acknowledgment messages.
tldr.mechanism: NORM uses selective Negative Acknowledgments (NACKs), where receivers only send a message if they detect a missing packet. The sender repairs losses by sending FEC parity symbols calculated from the original data. Feedback is suppressed using random timers so not all receivers send NACKs at once.
tldr.outcome: A sender can reliably deliver data to thousands or tens of thousands of receivers with manageable feedback traffic. NORM includes congestion control compatible with TCP and works over asymmetric networks (satellite, cable) where the return path is limited. It is experimental and was updated in RFC 5740.

today: RFC 3940 is Experimental. An updated protocol specification is provided in RFC 5740, which refines the NORM protocol based on experience and implementation feedback. NORM remains in use for research, military networks, and specialized multicast applications where bulk reliable delivery is required.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Goals
sections.content:
NORM is a protocol for reliable transport of bulk data (files or streams) over IP multicast networks. It is designed to efficiently scale to large receiver populations without overwhelming the sender with acknowledgment messages. The protocol operates over generic IP multicast routing and can work with asymmetric connectivity, such as a satellite downlink and terrestrial unicast return paths.

The core design uses selective Negative Acknowledgments: receivers send a message only when they detect a loss. By using random exponential backoff timers, multiple receivers suppress redundant NACKs so only a few reach the sender. The sender responds by transmitting FEC repair symbols (parity packets) that allow any receiver with losses to reconstruct missing data using math instead of requesting retransmission.
sections.eli5: Instead of everyone raising their hand to say 'I heard you,' people only raise their hand to say 'I missed that part.' The sender figures out the answer with a formula the whole class can use.

sections.title: Delivery Service and Object Types
sections.content:
NORM can reliably deliver three types of objects: NORM_OBJECT_DATA (static data in application memory), NORM_OBJECT_FILE (files from storage), and NORM_OBJECT_STREAM (continuous streams of undefined length, similar to TCP). Each sender maintains a unique 32-bit identifier (NormNodeId) so receivers can track which sender's data they are receiving.

Each object is segmented into FEC encoding blocks and symbols for transmission. When systematic FEC codes are used, the sender first transmits source symbols (original data) and then parity symbols. Receivers detect packet losses by tracking sequence numbers in the sender's messages. Unlike protocols that demand positive acknowledgment from every receiver, NORM only hears from receivers that experienced loss, making it fundamentally scalable.
sections.eli5: NORM can send a file once (like saving to a USB drive), a live stream (like a radio broadcast), or data stored in memory. Each receiver tracks what it got and speaks up only if it's missing something.

sections.title: Protocol Messages and Repair Process
sections.content:
A NORM sender transmits NORM_DATA messages carrying either original data (source symbols) or FEC repair symbols. The sender also sends NORM_CMD commands for congestion control, round-trip time estimation, and stream flushing. Receivers detect loss and reply with NORM_NACK messages requesting repair of specific missing packets. The sender aggregates NACKs from multiple receivers and computes FEC repair symbols covering all requested losses, then transmits the repairs.

To avoid overwhelming the sender, NORM uses timer-based feedback suppression. When a receiver detects a loss, it does not immediately send a NACK. Instead, it sets a random backoff timer and listens. If other receivers send the same NACK, the local receiver hears the request and cancels its transmission. The sender also advertises repair state to the group, allowing receivers to suppress redundant requests. This design allows NORM to scale to tens of thousands of receivers with feedback load less than a single TCP connection.
sections.eli5: When a listener misses something, they wait a random time before asking. If someone else asks first, they stay quiet. The teacher sends the answer to everyone who asked, using a formula that covers all the questions at once.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Fairness
sections.content:
NORM includes a baseline congestion control mechanism (NORM-CC) based on TCP-Friendly Multicast Congestion Control (TFMCC), which allows NORM flows to coexist fairly with TCP flows on the same network path. The sender estimates the slowest receiver's available bandwidth by monitoring feedback and adjusts its transmission rate accordingly. This ensures NORM does not consume more than its fair share of capacity and gives way when competing traffic appears.

Receivers provide explicit congestion control feedback via NORM_ACK messages in response to sender commands. This allows the sender to learn about the network state even from receivers that have no missing data. The protocol allows operation in three scenarios: single-channel with congestion control, multiple channels with rate adaptation, and controlled network environments where congestion is managed by other means (such as satellite or cable networks with provisioned bandwidth).
sections.eli5: NORM watches how fast data is flowing and slows down if a link gets congested, just like TCP does. It asks listeners about their network and adjusts speed so everyone gets a fair share.

sections.title: Key Features and Flexibility
sections.content:
Minimal coordination: Senders and receivers can dynamically join and leave sessions with little overhead. Each sender has a unique ID, allowing multiple senders to operate in the same session if the application layer coordinates them. Asymmetric operation: Works with unidirectional multicast (sender to receivers) and includes optional unicast feedback where receivers send NACKs directly to the sender, useful for satellite or asymmetric networks.

Additional features include round-trip time collection (the sender gathers RTT from feedback), positive acknowledgment options for applications requiring confirmation of receipt, and support for both IPv4 and IPv6. The protocol is tolerant of inaccurate timing and handles heavy packet loss and large delays, making it suitable for mobile and wireless networks. By design, NORM does not provide global identification of data content; applications must add that if needed.
sections.eli5: Multiple teachers can teach in the same session. It works even with one-way links (like satellites). It handles bad networks with lots of delays and lost packets. The system measures how fast each receiver's link is and adjusts accordingly.
